learning_objective: 🎯 Visualize 3D shapes combined together, and calculate their total surface areas and volumes for complex real-life objects!

main_concepts.simple_explanation: Real-life objects are often made by sticking basic 3D shapes together. For example, a test tube is a cylinder with a hemisphere at the bottom; a circus tent is a cylinder with a cone on top.

To find the Total Surface Area (TSA) of a combined solid, DO NOT just add the TSAs of the individual shapes. You only add the Curved Surface Areas (CSA) of the visible parts. Hidden faces (where they join) are excluded.
Unlike surface area, Volume is straightforward! The volume of a combined solid is simply the sum of the volumes of the individual constituent shapes.
You must memorize formulas for Cylinder (CSA=2πrh, Vol=πr²h), Cone (CSA=πrl, Vol=1/3 πr²h), Sphere (SA=4πr², Vol=4/3 πr³), and Hemisphere (CSA=2πr², Vol=2/3 πr³).

fun_activity.title: 🍦 The Ice Cream Anatomy
fun_activity.instructions: Look at an ice cream cone with a perfectly round scoop on top. It's a combination of a Cone and a Hemisphere! If the radius is 3cm, can you calculate the volume of ice cream you get?

exam_tips: 📌 Always write down the formulas you are using before plugging in the numbers. This secures formula marks.
📌 Remember the Pythagorean relation for the cone's slant height (l): l² = r² + h².
📌 Keep the π symbol as a variable until the very last step of your calculation. Often, π will cancel out or become easier to multiply at the end.
quick_recap: ⭐ Area is measured in square units (cm², m²), while Volume is measured in cubic units (cm³, m³).
⭐ The 'Total' Surface Area of a combined object uses the 'Curved' Surface Area formulas of its parts.
⭐ An open cylinder (like a pipe) only has a Curved Surface Area, no top or bottom bases.
